headline: Tesla recalls 3 million cars in China over hidden emergency door releases
summary: The recall addresses a safety concern where hidden manual door releases can trap occupants during emergencies, prompting both warning labels and software updates.
details: Tesla is recalling nearly 3 million vehicles in China to address hidden emergency door releases. This nationwide effort aims to prevent occupants from being trapped in crashes or fires.

This recall is part of a broader initiative involving 11 carmakers in China, including Xiaomi, Xpeng, Zeekr, and Lynk & Co. Companies will install warning labels and push software updates to improve safety.

The issue arises from the widespread use of electronic door latches, which can fail in a collision. While manual backups exist, they are often concealed or hard to access, posing a significant safety risk.

China plans to ban hidden, electronically-actuated exterior door handles from 2027, following a two-year review. US regulators are also investigating Tesla's door-latching system and considering new safety rules.
Other manufacturers like Rivian and Ford have faced similar challenges with manual releases. Rivian, for example, is redesigning its manual release for newer models after customer concerns.
Tesla, which popularized flush exterior handles and electronic latches, has stated it is working on redesigning its door handles for future vehicles to enhance accessibility and safety.

headline_marked: [[Top YouTube creators face backlash]] for promoting AI platform Higgsfield without disclosure
headline: Top YouTube creators face backlash for promoting AI platform Higgsfield without disclosure
summary: Prominent filmmakers like Matti Haapoja and Sam Kolder posted videos showcasing Higgsfield's AI tools, leading to fan alienation over alleged undisclosed paid partnerships and affiliate links.
details: Prominent YouTube filmmaking creators, including Matti Haapoja and Sam Kolder, recently posted videos demonstrating the capabilities of the AI platform Higgsfield. Their videos highlighted Higgsfield's Seedance 2.5 functionality, pitching these technologies as the future of video production.

This led to a significant backlash from fans and other creators, who shared screenshots of partnership offers from PR firms working for Higgsfield. Fans concluded that these were paid promotions, especially since the videos were not labeled as ads and neither the creators nor Higgsfield responded to inquiries about paid partnerships.

Haapoja's video resembled an infomercial, explaining how Higgsfield's feature-length film "Cully Hill Boys" was produced with AI prompts and showcasing Seedance 2.5. Kolder's video, titled "AI is replacing me," featured a fictionalized narrative exploring Mauritania with a robot, blending real footage with AI-generated imagery.

Critics, including Marques Brownlee, took issue with Haapoja comparing generative AI to the Canon EOS 5D Mark II. Brownlee emphasized that unlike the 5D Mark II, which is a physical tool, generative AI is trained on human-made material without credit or compensation.

While Kolder's video received a mixed response, with some positive comments, many viewers lamented that "AI defeated our king" and insisted that "no AI can replace creative artists." The core sentiment against AI replacing human creativity resonated strongly.

The intensity of the negative reactions to Haapoja's and Kolder's posts was notably higher than for other Higgsfield collaborations. This difference is largely attributed to the perception that these videos were sponsored advertisements designed to sway their audiences, with Kolder's caption even appearing to contain an affiliate link for a Higgsfield subscription.
